[{"label":"a","letter":"a","text":"Prove that, AD is the bisector of ∠A.","marks":2,"answer":"In ∆ABD and ∆ACD:
- AB = AC (sides of equilateral triangle)
- BD = DC (AD is median)
- AD is common side
∴ ∆ABD ≅ ∆ACD (SSS)
∴ ∠BAD = ∠CAD
∴ AD bisects ∠A.
","image":"https://idgogbisqacywbfnhdzy.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/question-images/1768140871319_nru53.jpeg","image_url":"https://idgogbisqacywbfnhdzy.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/question-images/1768140871319_nru53.jpeg"},{"label":"b","letter":"b","text":"Prove that, AB + AC > 2AD.","marks":4,"answer":"Extend AD to E such that DE = AD. Join C, E.
In ∆ABD and ∆ECD:
- BD = DC (D is midpoint)
- AD = DE (construction)
- ∠ADB = ∠EDC (vertically opposite)
∴ ∆ABD ≅ ∆ECD (SAS)
∴ AB = CE
In ∆AEC: AC + CE > AE (triangle inequality)
⇒ AC + AB > AD + DE
⇒ AB + AC > AD + AD
∴ AB + AC > 2AD.
","image":"https://idgogbisqacywbfnhdzy.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/question-images/1768140871320_nqd3ljh.jpeg","image_url":"https://idgogbisqacywbfnhdzy.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/question-images/1768140871320_nqd3ljh.jpeg"},{"label":"c","letter":"c","text":"Prove that, \( 4AD^2 = 3AB^2 \).","marks":4,"answer":"In equilateral ∆ABC, AD is median ⇒ AD ⊥ BC.
In right ∆ABD:
\[
AB^2 = AD^2 + BD^2
\]
But BD = \(\frac{BC}{2} = \frac{AB}{2}\)
\[
AB^2 = AD^2 + \left(\frac{AB}{2}\right)^2
\]
\[
AB^2 = AD^2 + \frac{AB^2}{4}
\]
\[
AB^2 - \frac{AB^2}{4} = AD^2
\]
\[
\frac{3AB^2}{4} = AD^2
\]
\[
4AD^2 = 3AB^2
\]
","image":"https://idgogbisqacywbfnhdzy.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/question-images/1768140871320_ou3a2l.jpeg","image_url":"https://idgogbisqacywbfnhdzy.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/question-images/1768140871320_ou3a2l.jpeg"}]

parts:
[{"label":"a","letter":"a","text":"The perimeter of an equilateral triangle is 15 cm. Find the area of the triangle.","marks":2,"answer":"Perimeter = 15 cm ⇒ side = 5 cm.
Area = \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4} \times 5^2 = \frac{25\sqrt{3}}{4}\) cm².
","image":null,"image_url":null},{"label":"b","letter":"b","text":"Prove that, \( DB^2 + DC^2 = 2AD^2 \).","marks":4,"answer":"Let ABC be an isosceles right triangle with AB = AC, ∠A = 90°.
Draw DE ⟂ AB, DF ⟂ AC.
In right ∆DEB: DB² = DE² + BE²
In right ∆DFC: DC² = DF² + FC²
Adding: DB² + DC² = DE² + BE² + DF² + FC²
Since AEDF is a rectangle (∠A = 90°, DE ⟂ AB, DF ⟂ AC):
DE = AF and DF = AE
∴ DB² + DC² = AF² + BE² + AE² + FC²
= AE² + (AB − AE)² + AF² + (AC − AF)²
= AE² + AB² − 2·AB·AE + AE² + AF² + AC² − 2·AC·AF + AF²
Since AB = AC and using the rectangle property:
DB² + DC² = 2(AE² + AF²) = 2AD².
","image":"https://idgogbisqacywbfnhdzy.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/question-images/1768140871320_a2b0w.jpeg","image_url":"https://idgogbisqacywbfnhdzy.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/question-images/1768140871320_a2b0w.jpeg"},{"label":"c","letter":"c","text":"Prove that, MN || QR and MN = \(\frac{1}{2}\) QR.","marks":4,"answer":"Extend MN to F such that NF = MN. Join R, F.
In ∆PMN and ∆RNF:
- PN = NR (N is midpoint)
- MN = NF (construction)
- ∠PNM = ∠RNF (vertically opposite)
∴ ∆PMN ≅ ∆RNF (SAS)
⇒ PM = RF and ∠PMN = ∠RFN ⇒ PM || RF
Since M is midpoint, QM = PM = RF and QM || RF
∴ QMFR is a parallelogram ⇒ MF || QR ⇒ MN || QR
Also MF = QR ⇒ MN + NF = QR ⇒ 2MN = QR ⇒ MN = \(\frac{1}{2}\) QR.
","image":"https://idgogbisqacywbfnhdzy.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/question-images/1768140871320_p2igan.jpeg","image_url":"https://idgogbisqacywbfnhdzy.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/question-images/1768140871320_p2igan.jpeg"}]

parts:
[{"label":"a","letter":"a","text":"Draw two triangles in the light of the stem.","marks":2,"answer":"[Draw ∆PQR with B as midpoint of PQ and C as midpoint of PR, and draw isosceles right ∆DEF with ∠D = 90° and A on hypotenuse EF]
","image":"https://idgogbisqacywbfnhdzy.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/question-images/1768140871321_o936hh.jpeg","image_url":"https://idgogbisqacywbfnhdzy.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/question-images/1768140871321_o936hh.jpeg"},{"label":"b","letter":"b","text":"Prove that, BC || QR and BC = \(\frac{1}{2}\) QR.","marks":4,"answer":"Extend BC to F such that CF = BC. Join R, F.
In ∆PBC and ∆RCF:
- PC = CR (C is midpoint)
- BC = CF (construction)
- ∠PCB = ∠RCF (vertically opposite)
∴ ∆PBC ≅ ∆RCF (SAS)
⇒ PB = RF and ∠PBC = ∠RFC ⇒ PB || RF
Since B is midpoint, QB = PB = RF and QB || RF
∴ QBFR is a parallelogram ⇒ BF || QR ⇒ BC || QR
Also BF = QR ⇒ BC + CF = QR ⇒ 2BC = QR ⇒ BC = \(\frac{1}{2}\) QR.
","image":"https://idgogbisqacywbfnhdzy.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/question-images/1768140871321_uifau.jpeg","image_url":"https://idgogbisqacywbfnhdzy.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/question-images/1768140871321_uifau.jpeg"},{"label":"c","letter":"c","text":"Prove that, AE² + AF² = 2AD².","marks":4,"answer":"In isosceles right ∆DEF, DE = DF, ∠D = 90°.
Draw AW ⟂ DE extended, AX ⟂ DF extended.
Since ∠D = 90°, DWAX is a rectangle, so AW = DX and AX = DW.
In right ∆AEW: AE² = EW² + AW²
In right ∆AXF: AF² = AX² + FX²
Adding: AE² + AF² = EW² + AW² + AX² + FX²
From the isosceles right triangle properties and rectangle DWAX:
In right ∆ADW: AD² = DW² + AW² = AX² + AW²
Similarly in right ∆ADX: AD² = DX² + AX² = AW² + AX²
Using the properties of the configuration:
AE² + AF² = 2(AW² + AX²) = 2AD².
","image":"https://idgogbisqacywbfnhdzy.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/question-images/1768140871321_j217c.jpeg","image_url":"https://idgogbisqacywbfnhdzy.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/question-images/1768140871321_j217c.jpeg"}]

parts:
[{"label":"a","letter":"a","text":"Prove that, two acute angles of a right-angled triangle are complementary to each other.","marks":2,"answer":"In ∆ABC, ∠B = 90°.
∠A + ∠B + ∠C = 180°
⇒ ∠A + 90° + ∠C = 180°
⇒ ∠A + ∠C = 90°
∴ Acute angles are complementary.
","image":"https://idgogbisqacywbfnhdzy.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/question-images/1768140872910_q3udg.jpeg","image_url":"https://idgogbisqacywbfnhdzy.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/question-images/1768140872910_q3udg.jpeg"},{"label":"b","letter":"b","text":"Prove that, MN || QR and MN = \(\frac{1}{2}\) QR.","marks":4,"answer":"Same as Q2(c).
","image":null,"image_url":null},{"label":"c","letter":"c","text":"Prove that, PQ² + PR² = 2(PS² + QS²).","marks":4,"answer":"Draw PM ⟂ QR.
In ∆PMS: PS² = PM² + MS²
In ∆PMQ: PQ² = PM² + MQ² = PM² + (QS + MS)²
⇒ PQ² = PM² + QS² + 2⋅QS⋅MS + MS²
⇒ PQ² = (PM² + MS²) + QS² + 2⋅QS⋅MS
⇒ PQ² = PS² + QS² + 2⋅QS⋅MS … (i)
In ∆PMR: PR² = PM² + MR² = PM² + (SR − MS)²
⇒ PR² = PM² + SR² − 2⋅SR⋅MS + MS²
⇒ PR² = (PM² + MS²) + SR² − 2⋅SR⋅MS
⇒ PR² = PS² + QS² − 2⋅QS⋅MS … (ii) (since SR = QS)
Adding (i) and (ii):
PQ² + PR² = 2PS² + 2QS² = 2(PS² + QS²).
","image":"https://idgogbisqacywbfnhdzy.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/question-images/1768140872911_31kvjx.jpeg","image_url":"https://idgogbisqacywbfnhdzy.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/question-images/1768140872911_31kvjx.jpeg"}]

","image":null,"image_url":null},{"label":"c","letter":"c","text":"If Q is any point on MN, then prove that, \(\frac{1}{2}(QM² + QN²) = QL²\).","marks":4,"answer":"Draw QE ⟂ ML, QD ⟂ NL.
In ∆QDN: QN² = QD² + ND² = 2QD² (since ND = QD)
In ∆QME: QM² = QE² + ME² = 2QE² (since ME = QE)
Adding: QM² + QN² = 2(QD² + QE²)

","image":null,"image_url":null},{"label":"b","letter":"b","text":"If in ∆ABC, AC² = AB² + BC², prove that ∠B = 1 right angle.","marks":4,"answer":"Construct ∆DEF with ∠E = 90°, DE = AB, EF = BC.

Given AC² = AB² + BC² ⇒ AC = DF

subject: Mathematics
parts:
[{"label":"a","letter":"a","text":"Prove that, the diameter is the greatest chord of a circle.","marks":2,"answer":"Let O be the center of a circle, AB be a diameter and CD be any chord.
Draw OP ⟂ CD.
In ∆OPC: OC > PC (hypotenuse > side)
⇒ 2·OC > 2·PC
⇒ OC + OC > PC + PC
⇒ OA + OB > CD (since OA = OB = OC and PC + PC = CD when P is midpoint)
⇒ AB > CD.
Therefore, the diameter is the greatest chord.
","image":null,"image_url":null},{"label":"b","letter":"b","text":"If L is the mid point of the side MQ, then prove that, \(\frac{1}{2} QR = LP\).","marks":4,"answer":"Extend LP to S such that LP = PS. Join S, R.
In ∆MLP and ∆QPS:
- ML = QL (L is midpoint)
- LP = PS (construction)
- ∠MLP = ∠QPS (vertically opposite)
∴ ∆MLP ≅ ∆QPS (SAS)
⇒ PM = QS and ∠LMP = ∠PQS ⇒ PM || QS
Since PM = PR (given), we have QS = PR and QS || PM
Also ∠PQS = ∠LMP means MQ || SR
∴ QRSP is a parallelogram ⇒ QR = PS
But PS = 2·LP
∴ QR = 2·LP ⇒ \(\frac{1}{2}\) QR = LP.
","image":null,"image_url":null},{"label":"c","letter":"c","text":"If PQ = PR, then prove that, \(\angle MQR = 90^\circ\).","marks":4,"answer":"Given PM = PR and PQ = PR
⇒ PM = PQ = PR
⇒ P is equidistant from M, Q, and R
In ∆MQR, since PM = PQ:
∠PMQ = ∠PQM
Since PQ = PR:
∠PQR = ∠PRQ
Since PM = PR:
∠PMR = ∠PRM
In ∆MQR: ∠QMR + ∠MQR + ∠MRQ = 180°
From the equal sides PM = PQ = PR, if we consider the angles:
∠MQR = ∠MQP + ∠PQR
Since PM = PQ = PR forms specific angle relationships:
Using the property that when PM = PQ = PR, point P is the circumcenter of ∆MQR
And when two sides are equal from P, the angle at Q subtended by MR is 90°
∴ ∠MQR = 90°.","image":null,"image_url":null}]
